prompt: According to VSEPR, what sets the arrangement of the electron pairs around a central atom?

choices.text: Electron pairs are negatively charged, so they repel each other and get as far apart as possible.
Electron pairs attract each other, so they cluster together on one side of the central atom.
choices.why: Electron pairs are made of negatively charged particles, and like charges repel. VSEPR says they spread as far apart as possible.

choices.text: The surrounding atoms repel each other, and the electron pairs simply follow the atoms.
choices.why: VSEPR is based on repulsion between electron pairs, not atoms. That is why lone pairs, which have no atom attached, still affect the shape.

choices.text: Only bonding pairs repel each other, so lone pairs have no effect on where the bonds point.
choices.why: Lone pairs are electron groups too. They take up positions around the central atom just as bonds do.

explanation: Valence shell electron pair repulsion (VSEPR) says that electron pairs, being made of negatively charged particles, repel each other and get as far away from each other as possible. That arrangement is the basis of a molecule's shape.

prompt: VSEPR recognizes two types of electron groups. What are they?

choices.text: Bonds of any type, and lone pairs of electrons
Single bonds, and multiple bonds
choices.why: Single, double, and triple bonds are all one type of electron group: a bond. This choice leaves out the other type, lone pairs.

choices.text: Bonds to hydrogen atoms, and bonds to all other atoms
choices.why: Every bond is the same type of group, whatever atom it goes to. The second type is a lone pair.

choices.text: Bonding pairs, and inner-shell (core) electrons
choices.why: VSEPR deals with the valence shell only. The second type of electron group is a lone pair of valence electrons.

explanation: The two types of electron groups are bonds, whether single, double, or triple, and lone electron pairs. Each bond counts as one group, and so does each lone pair on the central atom.

prompt: How does molecular geometry differ from electron group geometry?

choices.text: Molecular geometry describes how the atoms are arranged; electron group geometry describes how the bonds and lone pairs are arranged.
Molecular geometry describes how the bonds and lone pairs are arranged; electron group geometry describes how the atoms are arranged.
choices.why: This reverses the two. Electron group geometry includes the lone pairs; molecular geometry describes only where the atoms are.

choices.text: They are two names for the same arrangement, so they always give the same shape name.
choices.why: They differ whenever the central atom has lone pairs. H2O, for example, has a tetrahedral electron group geometry but a bent shape.

choices.text: Molecular geometry counts only single bonds, while electron group geometry also counts double and triple bonds.
choices.why: Every bond, single or multiple, is one electron group. The two geometries differ in whether lone pairs are part of the description, not in which bonds count.

explanation: Electron group geometry expresses how the electron groups (bonds and lone pairs) are arranged around the central atom. Molecular geometry expresses how the atoms are arranged. The two are related, but they are not always the same.

prompt: Three-dimensional molecules are often drawn on paper using straight lines, solid wedges, and dashed wedges for bonds. What does a solid wedge show?

choices.text: A bond coming out of the plane of the page toward the reader
A bond going back behind the page, away from the reader
choices.why: That is what a dashed wedge shows. A solid wedge points out of the page, toward you.

choices.text: A bond lying flat in the plane of the page
choices.why: Bonds in the plane of the page are drawn as ordinary straight lines.

choices.text: A double bond between the central atom and a surrounding atom
choices.why: Wedges show direction in three dimensions, not the number of shared pairs. A double bond is drawn as two lines.

explanation: In this convention, straight lines lie in the plane of the page, a solid wedge comes out of the plane toward the reader, and a dashed wedge goes back out of the plane away from the reader.

prompt: According to the section, the shapes of which molecules can be easily predicted?

choices.text: Small molecules with a single central atom
Only molecules made of exactly two atoms
choices.why: VSEPR also predicts the shapes of larger molecules, such as CH4 and NH3, as long as they have one central atom.

choices.text: Only molecules whose central atom has no lone pairs
choices.why: Lone pairs are part of the method. They count as electron groups, as in NH3 and H2O.

choices.text: Large molecules with several central atoms
choices.why: The section says the easily predicted shapes are those of small molecules, the ones with a single central atom.

explanation: Small molecules, those with a single central atom, have shapes that can be easily predicted with VSEPR by looking at the electron groups on that central atom.

prompt: BF3 is a trigonal planar molecule: its B atom is bonded to three F atoms and has no lone pairs. What is the F–B–F bond angle, in degrees?
explanation: Three electron groups get as far apart as possible by taking the positions of an equilateral triangle in one plane, 120° apart. All three are bonded to F atoms, so each F–B–F angle is 120°.

prompt: According to the section, which two things let you predict the approximate shape of a molecule with a single central atom?

choices.text: The number of electron groups on the central atom and the number of surrounding atoms
The total number of valence electrons and the total number of bonds in the molecule
choices.why: Those counts are used to draw the Lewis diagram. The shape is then predicted from the central atom's electron groups and how many atoms surround it.

choices.text: The number of single bonds and the number of double bonds in the molecule
choices.why: Bond counts alone leave out the lone pairs on the central atom. The shape depends on all of the central atom's electron groups and on how many atoms surround it.

choices.text: The kinds of elements bonded to the central atom and the polarity of each bond
choices.why: The approximate shape comes from counts alone, the electron groups and the surrounding atoms, whatever elements they are.

explanation: The approximate shape of a molecule can be predicted from the number of electron groups on the central atom and the number of surrounding atoms. The first count sets the electron group geometry; the second says which positions hold atoms.

prompt: What shows that molecules really do have shapes?

choices.text: Experimental evidence, from their physical properties to their chemical reactivity
The way their Lewis electron dot diagrams are drawn on paper
choices.why: Lewis diagrams are drawn flat and show which atoms are bonded, not the real three-dimensional shape. The evidence for shapes comes from experiments.

choices.text: Their chemical formulas, which show how the atoms are arranged
choices.why: A formula gives the number of each kind of atom, not their arrangement in space.

choices.text: Nothing; molecular shapes are only a convenient idea for drawing
choices.why: The section says there is an abundance of experimental evidence that molecules have shapes.

explanation: There is an abundance of experimental evidence that molecules have shapes, from their physical properties to their chemical reactivity. VSEPR is a way to predict those shapes.

prompt: When you count the electron groups on a central atom, how many groups does a double bond count as, and why?

choices.text: One, because both of its shared pairs lie between the same two atoms
Two, because it contains two shared pairs of electrons
choices.why: A multiple bond counts as only one electron group. Both of its shared pairs connect the central atom to the same atom, so they occupy one position.

choices.text: One, because only one of its two pairs is actually shared
choices.why: Both pairs in a double bond are shared between the two atoms. It counts as one group because both pairs connect the same two atoms.

choices.text: Zero, because multiple bonds do not repel other electron groups
choices.why: Every bond is an electron group, and electron pairs always repel one another. A double bond counts as one group.

explanation: Any bond, single, double, or triple, counts as one electron group. All the shared pairs of a double bond lie between the central atom and the same surrounding atom, so together they occupy one position around the central atom.

prompt: The four electron groups on the N atom of NH3 point toward the corners of a tetrahedron, yet the shape of NH3 is called trigonal pyramidal, not tetrahedral. Why?

choices.text: The shape describes only where the atoms are, and one of the four groups is a lone pair with no atom.
A lone pair doesn't count as an electron group, so N really has only three groups.
choices.why: A lone pair is an electron group. N has four groups, which is why they point toward a tetrahedron.

choices.text: The three N–H bonds pull the H atoms into a flat triangle around the N atom.
choices.why: A flat triangle would be trigonal planar. The lone pair still takes one corner of the tetrahedron, so the atoms form a pyramid.

choices.text: Bonds to H atoms are not counted when a molecular shape is named.
choices.why: Every surrounding atom counts in the molecular shape, H atoms included. NH3 has three surrounding atoms.

explanation: The electron group geometry includes the lone pair, so it is tetrahedral. The molecular geometry describes only the atoms; with atoms on just three of the four positions, the N atom and the three H atoms form a trigonal pyramid.

prompt: The Lewis diagram of CCl4 is usually drawn flat, with the four Cl atoms above, below, left, and right of the C atom. Why does VSEPR place the Cl atoms at the corners of a tetrahedron instead of at the corners of a flat square?

choices.text: Pointing toward the corners of a tetrahedron puts the four electron groups farther apart than a flat square does.
The C atom has a lone pair that pushes the four C–Cl bonds out of the plane.
choices.why: C uses all four of its valence electrons in the four C–Cl bonds and has no lone pair. The four bonds alone spread out into a tetrahedron.

choices.text: The four C–Cl bonds attract one another, so they bend toward the same side of the C atom.
choices.why: Electron groups repel one another; they don't attract. Repulsion spreads them as far apart as possible.

choices.text: The flat square is the real shape; the tetrahedron is only a way of drawing it in three dimensions.
choices.why: The tetrahedron is the molecule's real shape. A Lewis diagram shows which atoms are bonded, not how they are arranged in space.

explanation: A Lewis diagram shows which atoms are bonded, not the shape. Four electron groups repel each other and get as far apart as possible by pointing toward the corners of a tetrahedron, which spreads them farther apart than a flat square would.

prompt: In hydrogen cyanide, HCN, the C atom is the central atom, bonded to the H atom and to the N atom. How many electron groups are around the central C atom?
explanation: HCN has 1 + 4 + 5 = 10 valence electrons. Giving C an octet takes a single bond to H and a triple bond to N, with no lone pairs on C. The triple bond counts as one group, so C has 2 electron groups.

prompt: In sulfur dioxide, SO2, the S atom is the central atom, bonded to both O atoms. How many electron groups are around the central S atom?
explanation: SO2 has 6 + 2(6) = 18 valence electrons. S is double-bonded to one O atom, single-bonded to the other, and has one lone pair. Two bonds plus one lone pair make 3 electron groups.

prompt: A student's Lewis diagram of H2S shows S bonded to two H atoms with one lone pair on S, so the student says H2S has a trigonal planar electron group geometry and a bent shape. What is wrong?

choices.text: S has two lone pairs, so it has four electron groups: the electron group geometry is tetrahedral, though the shape is still bent.
Nothing is wrong: S has three electron groups, two of them bonds, so H2S is bent with trigonal planar electron groups.
choices.why: H2S has 8 valence electrons. Two S–H bonds use 4, leaving 4 electrons, two lone pairs, on S. S has four electron groups, not three.

choices.text: S has no lone pairs at all, so it has only two electron groups, and H2S is actually linear rather than bent.
choices.why: S has six valence electrons and uses only two of them in bonds. The other four form two lone pairs, which make the molecule bent.

choices.text: S has two lone pairs, so it has four electron groups, and the molecular shape of H2S is therefore tetrahedral.
choices.why: The electron group geometry is tetrahedral, but the molecular shape describes only the atoms. With two atoms bonded to S, H2S is bent.

explanation: H2S has 2(1) + 6 = 8 valence electrons: two S–H bonds use 4, and the other 4 are two lone pairs on S, giving it an octet. Four electron groups give a tetrahedral electron group geometry, and with only two of them holding atoms, H2S is bent.

prompt: In hypochlorous acid, HOCl, the O atom is the central atom, bonded to the H atom and to the Cl atom. How many lone pairs are on the central O atom?
explanation: HOCl has 1 + 6 + 7 = 14 valence electrons. The two single bonds use 4 and completing the Cl octet uses 6, so the remaining 4 electrons are 2 lone pairs on O, giving it an octet.

prompt: Carbon disulfide, CS2, has a central C atom bonded to two S atoms. What is the S–C–S bond angle, in degrees?
explanation: To give every atom an octet, C forms a double bond to each S atom and has no lone pairs. Each double bond is one electron group, so C has two groups, 180° apart, and the S atoms are 180° apart too: CS2 is linear.

prompt: Nitrogen trifluoride, NF3, has a central N atom bonded to three F atoms. What are its electron group geometry and its molecular shape?

choices.text: Electron group geometry tetrahedral; molecular shape trigonal pyramidal
Electron group geometry trigonal pyramidal; molecular shape tetrahedral
choices.why: These are reversed. The four electron groups (three bonds and a lone pair) are arranged tetrahedrally; the atoms alone form a trigonal pyramid.

choices.text: Electron group geometry trigonal planar; molecular shape trigonal planar
choices.why: This leaves out the lone pair on N. N has four electron groups, not three.

choices.text: Electron group geometry tetrahedral; molecular shape tetrahedral
choices.why: The molecular shape describes only the atoms. One of the four groups is a lone pair, so the four atoms form a trigonal pyramid.

explanation: NF3 has 5 + 3(7) = 26 valence electrons; after three N–F bonds and octets on the F atoms, 2 electrons remain as a lone pair on N. Four electron groups give a tetrahedral electron group geometry, and with three of them bonded to atoms, the molecule is trigonal pyramidal.

prompt: In ozone, O3, one O atom is the central atom, bonded to the other two O atoms. What are the electron group geometry and the molecular shape of O3?

choices.text: Electron group geometry trigonal planar; molecular shape bent
Electron group geometry linear; molecular shape linear
choices.why: This misses the lone pair on the central O atom. It has two bonds and one lone pair: three electron groups.

choices.text: Electron group geometry tetrahedral; molecular shape bent
choices.why: The central O has only one lone pair. With one double bond and one single bond, it has three electron groups, not four.

choices.text: Electron group geometry trigonal planar; molecular shape trigonal planar
choices.why: Only two of the three groups hold atoms. The molecular shape describes the atoms, so O3 is bent.

explanation: O3 has 3 × 6 = 18 valence electrons. The central O is double-bonded to one outer O, single-bonded to the other, and has one lone pair: three electron groups, so its electron group geometry is trigonal planar. Only two groups hold atoms, so O3 is bent.

prompt: A molecule with a single central atom has a trigonal planar electron group geometry, but its molecular shape is bent. How many lone pairs are on the central atom?
explanation: A trigonal planar electron group geometry means three electron groups. A bent shape means only two of them are bonded to atoms, so the third group is 1 lone pair.

prompt: For which molecule are the electron group geometry and the molecular shape the same?

choices.text: CF4
NH3
choices.why: N has three bonds and one lone pair. Its electron group geometry is tetrahedral, but its shape is trigonal pyramidal.

choices.text: H2O
choices.why: O has two bonds and two lone pairs. Its electron group geometry is tetrahedral, but its shape is bent.

choices.text: NOF
choices.why: N has two bonds and one lone pair. Its electron group geometry is trigonal planar, but its shape is bent.

explanation: In CF4, C has four bonds to F atoms and no lone pairs, so every one of its four electron groups holds an atom. Both the electron group geometry and the molecular shape are tetrahedral.

prompt: A student reasons that each C=O bond in CO2 has two shared pairs, so the C atom has four electron groups, two of them bonded to O atoms, and CO2 must be bent. What is wrong with this reasoning?

choices.text: Each double bond counts as only one electron group, so C has two groups and CO2 is linear.
C has four electron groups, but all four are bonded to O atoms, so CO2 is tetrahedral.
choices.why: There are only two O atoms, and each double bond is one electron group. C has two groups, both bonded to O.

choices.text: C has two electron groups, but they are 120° apart, so CO2 is bent.
choices.why: Two electron groups get as far apart as possible, on opposite sides of the C atom, so CO2 is linear.

choices.text: Nothing is wrong; four electron groups with two surrounding atoms give a bent molecule.
choices.why: That rule is right, but the count is wrong. A double bond counts as one group, so C has only two.

explanation: A multiple bond counts as only one electron group. C in CO2 has two double bonds and no lone pairs, so it has two electron groups, which get as far apart as possible, and the molecule is linear.

prompt: A student notes that the Br atom in HBr has four electron groups around it and concludes that HBr is tetrahedral. What is wrong with this conclusion?

choices.text: HBr has only two atoms, and any molecule with only two atoms is linear.
Br has only one electron group, because lone pairs are not electron groups.
choices.why: Lone pairs are electron groups, so Br does have four (one bond and three lone pairs). The shape is linear because only one atom is attached.

choices.text: Br has four electron groups, but HBr is bent because three of them are lone pairs.
choices.why: A bent shape needs two atoms bonded to a central atom. HBr has only two atoms in all, so it is linear.

choices.text: Br's four electron groups point toward the corners of a flat square, not a tetrahedron.
choices.why: Four electron groups do point toward a tetrahedron. The error is naming the molecular shape from the electron groups instead of from the atoms.

explanation: Molecular shape describes where the atoms are. Br's four electron groups (one bond and three lone pairs) point toward a tetrahedron, but only one holds an atom, so the two atoms of HBr lie on a straight line: linear.

prompt: A student says PH3 must be trigonal planar because its central P atom is bonded to three H atoms. What did the student overlook?

choices.text: P also has a lone pair, so it has four electron groups and PH3 is trigonal pyramidal.
P forms a double bond to one of the H atoms, so PH3 is bent.
choices.why: An H atom can make only one bond. P has three single bonds to H atoms and one lone pair.

choices.text: Each H atom carries a lone pair, so PH3 is tetrahedral.
choices.why: An H atom has only the one pair it shares with P and no lone pairs. The lone pair that matters is on P.

choices.text: Nothing; a central atom bonded to three atoms is always trigonal planar.
choices.why: That holds only when the central atom has three electron groups. P has a fourth group, a lone pair, which makes PH3 trigonal pyramidal.

explanation: PH3 has 5 + 3(1) = 8 valence electrons; three P–H bonds use 6, and the last 2 are a lone pair on P. Four electron groups point toward a tetrahedron, but only three hold atoms, so PH3 is trigonal pyramidal, not trigonal planar.

prompt: BeH2 and OF2 each have a central atom bonded to two atoms, but one molecule is linear and the other is bent. Which statement explains this?

choices.text: Be has two electron groups and no lone pairs, while O has two bonds and two lone pairs, so OF2 is bent.
O has two electron groups and Be has four, so BeH2 is bent and OF2 is linear.
choices.why: This reverses them. Be makes two bonds and has no lone pairs, while O has two lone pairs as well as two bonds, giving it four groups.

choices.text: F atoms are much larger than H atoms, so they crowd each other into a bent shape.
choices.why: The shape comes from the number of electron groups on the central atom, not from the sizes of the surrounding atoms.

choices.text: OF2 has polar bonds, and polar bonds always bend a molecule.
choices.why: Bond polarity doesn't set the shape; CO2 has polar bonds and is linear. OF2 is bent because of the lone pairs on O.

explanation: Be in BeH2 forms two bonds and has no lone pairs, so it has two electron groups and BeH2 is linear. O in OF2 has two bonds and two lone pairs; its four groups point toward a tetrahedron, and with only two holding atoms, OF2 is bent.

prompt: In carbonyl fluoride, COF2, the central C atom is double-bonded to the O atom and single-bonded to each of two F atoms, with no lone pairs. A student claims the molecule must be a perfect equilateral triangle, with all three bond angles equal. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: It is approximately trigonal planar, but the angles are not all equal, because the C=O bond differs from the C–F bonds.
The student is right: three electron groups on a central atom always form a perfect equilateral triangle.
choices.why: That holds when the three groups are alike. Here the C=O double bond differs from the two C–F single bonds, so the triangle is only approximate.

choices.text: It is tetrahedral, because the double bond to O counts as two electron groups on the C atom.
choices.why: A double bond counts as one electron group. C has three groups, all bonded to atoms, so the shape is approximately trigonal planar.

choices.text: It is trigonal pyramidal, because the C atom has a lone pair in addition to its three bonds.
choices.why: C uses all four of its valence electrons in bonding (two in the double bond and one in each single bond), so it has no lone pair.

explanation: C has three electron groups, all bonded to atoms, so COF2 is trigonal planar. Because the C=O double bond is different from the two C–F single bonds, the triangle is not perfectly equilateral, but planar and triangular still describe its approximate shape.

prompt: Which two molecules have the same molecular shape?

choices.text: SiH4 and CHF3
NH3 and CH2O
choices.why: NH3 is trigonal pyramidal (four electron groups, three atoms), but CH2O is trigonal planar (three electron groups, three atoms).

choices.text: CBr4 and PCl3
choices.why: CBr4 is tetrahedral, but PCl3 is trigonal pyramidal because P has a lone pair as well as three bonds.

choices.text: BF3 and NOF
choices.why: Both central atoms have three electron groups, but BF3 has three surrounding atoms (trigonal planar) while NOF has two (bent).

explanation: In SiH4, Si has four bonds to H atoms; in CHF3, C has bonds to one H atom and three F atoms. Each central atom has four electron groups, all bonded to atoms, so both molecules are tetrahedral, even though the surrounding atoms in CHF3 are not all alike.

prompt: A student counting the electron groups in SiCl4 adds the four Si–Cl bonds to the 12 lone pairs on the Cl atoms and gets 16 electron groups. What is the mistake?

choices.text: Only the electron groups on the central atom count, so Si has four groups and SiCl4 is tetrahedral.
Each Cl atom's three lone pairs count together as one group, so Si has eight electron groups.
choices.why: Lone pairs on the surrounding Cl atoms are not counted at all. Si has four electron groups: its four bonds.

choices.text: The bonds should not be counted, so SiCl4 has 12 electron groups, all of them lone pairs.
choices.why: Bonds are electron groups. The groups that set the shape are the central atom's: four bonds and no lone pairs.

choices.text: The count of 16 is right, but only the four bonded groups affect the shape of SiCl4.
choices.why: The Cl lone pairs are never electron groups of Si, so 16 is not the right count. Si has exactly four.

explanation: VSEPR counts the electron groups around the central atom only. Si in SiCl4 has four single bonds and no lone pairs, so it has four electron groups, all bonded to Cl atoms, and the molecule is tetrahedral. The lone pairs on the Cl atoms belong to the Cl atoms.

prompt: The electron groups on the central atom of a molecule point toward the corners of a tetrahedron, and at least two atoms are bonded to the central atom. Which list gives every molecular shape the molecule could have?

choices.text: Tetrahedral, trigonal pyramidal, or bent
Tetrahedral only
choices.why: The shape is tetrahedral only when all four groups hold atoms. When some groups are lone pairs, the shape is named from the atoms alone.

choices.text: Tetrahedral, trigonal planar, or bent
choices.why: Trigonal planar requires three electron groups. Four groups with three surrounding atoms give a trigonal pyramid, not a flat triangle.

choices.text: Trigonal pyramidal or bent only
choices.why: If all four groups hold atoms, as in CH4, the molecular shape is also tetrahedral.

explanation: Four electron groups point toward a tetrahedron. With four, three, or two surrounding atoms, the molecular shape is tetrahedral, trigonal pyramidal, or bent.

prompt: A molecule has a single central atom with four electron groups, two of which are lone pairs. How many atoms does the molecule contain in all, counting the central atom?
explanation: The two electron groups that are not lone pairs are bonds, each to one surrounding atom. Two surrounding atoms plus the central atom make 3 atoms, as in a bent molecule like H2O.

prompt: Two molecules, each with a single central atom, have the same electron group geometry. What must they also have in common?

choices.text: The same number of electron groups on the central atom
The same number of atoms bonded to the central atom
choices.why: Electron groups include lone pairs as well as bonds. CH4 and H2O both have a tetrahedral electron group geometry, but four and two surrounding atoms.

choices.text: The same molecular shape
choices.why: Molecular shape depends on how many groups hold atoms. CH4 and H2O share a tetrahedral electron group geometry, yet CH4 is tetrahedral and H2O is bent.

choices.text: The same number of lone pairs on the central atom
choices.why: The groups can be split differently between bonds and lone pairs: C in CH4 has no lone pairs, while O in H2O has two.

explanation: Electron group geometry is set by the number of electron groups alone. Two molecules with the same electron group geometry have the same number of groups, though those groups can be divided differently between bonds and lone pairs.
